title: KMP prefix function
prompt: Write prefixFunction(s string) []int, the KMP failure table: pi[i] is the length of the longest proper prefix of s[:i+1] that is also a suffix of it (proper means shorter than i+1). An empty string gives an empty slice. It must run in O(n): the tests feed a 250000-byte two-letter string, where re-testing candidate border lengths at each position is O(n^2) and never finishes.
explanation: The whole algorithm is one idea: the best border of s[:i+1] is one of the borders of s[:i] extended by s[i], and the borders of a prefix are exactly pi[i-1], pi[pi[i-1]-1], ... down to 0. So you never search, you walk that chain. Each iteration of the inner loop strictly decreases k and k only ever grows by one per outer step, so the total inner work is bounded by n: the same amortised argument as a monotonic stack. Once you have pi you get substring search for free by running the same loop over pattern + separator + text and reporting every position where the value reaches len(pattern), which is what the large test does. The separator matters: without a byte that appears nowhere else, a border could straddle the join and report a match that is not there.
hints: When a character fails to extend the current candidate, is there a shorter candidate you already computed rather than starting over?
What is the chain of all borders of a prefix, and which table already stores it?
Count how many times the value can grow versus how many times it can shrink across the whole scan.

title: Minimum spanning tree weight
prompt: Write minimumSpanningTree(n int, edges [][]int) int: the total weight of a minimum spanning tree of an undirected graph on vertices 0..n-1, where each edge is []int{u, v, w}. Return -1 if the graph is not connected, and 0 when n is 1. Duplicate edges and multiple edges between the same pair are allowed. The tests feed 300000 vertices and a million edges, so picking the next vertex by scanning all of them is too slow.
explanation: Kruskal is the cut property applied greedily: sort the edges and take each one that joins two components that are still separate. The part people get wrong is the membership test. Marking endpoints as 'seen' looks equivalent and is not, because two already-seen vertices can still be in different components, so the tree comes out disconnected or overweight; that is exactly what the random cross-check against the dense reference catches. Union-find with path compression and union by size makes each test effectively constant, so the run is dominated by the sort at O(m log m). Stopping after n-1 edges is what turns 'ran out of edges' into the disconnected answer without a second pass.
hints: After sorting, what question do you have to answer about an edge before you take it, and is 'have I touched these vertices before' the same question?
How many edges does a spanning tree of n vertices have, and what does running out before that tell you?
Which structure answers 'same component?' and 'merge these components' fast enough to be called a million times?

title: Walks of length k by matrix power
prompt: Write countWalks(adj [][]int, k int, mod int) int: the number of walks of exactly k edges from vertex 0 to vertex n-1 in a directed graph given by its adjacency matrix, taken modulo mod (mod is at least 2, and adj is square with n up to about 100). A walk may repeat vertices and edges. k is up to 10^18, so stepping the distribution forward one edge at a time is not an option.
explanation: Entry [i][j] of A^k is the number of walks of length k from i to j: the definition of matrix multiplication is exactly 'sum over the middle vertex', so multiplying the k-step matrix by A appends one more edge. That makes the answer A^k[0][n-1], and because matrix multiplication is associative you can get A^k with about log2(k) squarings instead of k multiplications: 60 squarings for k near 10^18 rather than a billion billion steps. Two details bite. Reduce inside the innermost loop, not at the end, or the counts overflow long before k=40 on a dense graph. And A^0 is the identity, so k=0 must answer 1 only when the start is the target, which is what makes the recurrence base case right rather than a special case bolted on.
hints: What does one entry of the product of two step-count matrices mean, if you read the multiplication formula as a sum over a middle vertex?
You cannot afford k multiplications, but how many do you need if you are allowed to reuse a result you already have?
Where must the modulus be applied so that no intermediate value ever exceeds what an int can hold?
